title: 202. Algebra, Equations & Inequalities: Solving Radical Equations with Verification
description: A comprehensive mathematics curriculum progressing from foundational numeracy and core mathematical concepts to algebra, geometry, calculus, linear algebra, probability, statistics, discrete mathematics, optimization, mathematical foundations of AI, advanced pure mathematics, and emerging research methods.

questions.learningObjective: Solve a simple radical equation by squaring both sides and verifying the solution.
questions.question: Solve \(\sqrt{x+5}=3\).
questions.explanation: Square both sides: \(x+5=9\), so \(x=4\). Check in the original equation: \(\sqrt{4+5}=\sqrt{9}=3\), so \(x=4\) is valid. The value \(x=-4\) would give \(\sqrt{1}=1\), not \(3\).
questions.hint: Isolate the radical if needed, then square both sides and check the result in the original equation.

questions.concept: Solving radical equations with a linear radical
questions.learningObjective: Solve a radical equation by squaring both sides and checking the domain.
questions.question: Solve \(\sqrt{2x-1}=x\).
questions.explanation: The domain requires \(2x-1\ge0\), so \(x\ge\frac{1}{2}\). Square both sides: \(2x-1=x^2\). Then \(x^2-2x+1=0\), so \((x-1)^2=0\), giving \(x=1\). Check: \(\sqrt{2(1)-1}=\sqrt{1}=1\), so \(x=1\) is valid. The value \(x=-1\) is not in the domain.
questions.hint: Square both sides, then check whether the result satisfies the original radical equation.

questions.learningObjective: Identify and discard an extraneous solution after squaring both sides.
questions.question: Solve \(\sqrt{x+7}=x-5\).
questions.explanation: Square both sides: \(x+7=x^2-10x+25\). Rearranging gives \(x^2-11x+18=0\), so \((x-2)(x-9)=0\). The candidates are \(x=2\) and \(x=9\). Check \(x=2\): \(\sqrt{9}=3\), but \(2-5=-3\), so it is extraneous. Check \(x=9\): \(\sqrt{16}=4\), and \(9-5=4\), so \(x=9\) is the only valid solution.
questions.hint: After squaring, test each candidate in the original equation, especially when the right side can be negative.

questions.concept: Radical equations with two valid solutions
questions.learningObjective: Solve a radical equation whose squared equation gives two valid solutions.
questions.question: Solve \(\sqrt{3x+1}=x+1\).
questions.explanation: Square both sides: \(3x+1=x^2+2x+1\). Then \(x^2-x=0\), so \(x(x-1)=0\). The candidates are \(x=0\) and \(x=1\). Check \(x=0\): \(\sqrt{1}=1\), and \(0+1=1\). Check \(x=1\): \(\sqrt{4}=2\), and \(1+1=2\). Both are valid.
questions.hint: Square both sides, factor the resulting quadratic, and verify each candidate in the original equation.

questions.learningObjective: Solve a radical equation and verify that both obtained values satisfy the original equation.
questions.question: Solve \(\sqrt{5x-1}=x+1\).
questions.explanation: Square both sides: \(5x-1=x^2+2x+1\). Then \(x^2-3x+2=0\), so \((x-1)(x-2)=0\). The candidates are \(x=1\) and \(x=2\). Check \(x=1\): \(\sqrt{4}=2\), and \(1+1=2\). Check \(x=2\): \(\sqrt{9}=3\), and \(2+1=3\). Both are valid.
questions.hint: Square both sides, solve the quadratic, and check both results in the original equation.

questions.concept: Rejecting an extraneous solution from a radical equation
questions.learningObjective: Determine the valid solution after squaring a radical equation that produces an extraneous value.
questions.question: Solve \(\sqrt{x+3}=x-3\).
questions.explanation: Square both sides: \(x+3=x^2-6x+9\). Then \(x^2-7x+6=0\), so \((x-1)(x-6)=0\). The candidates are \(x=1\) and \(x=6\). Check \(x=1\): \(\sqrt{4}=2\), but \(1-3=-2\), so it is extraneous. Check \(x=6\): \(\sqrt{9}=3\), and \(6-3=3\). Thus only \(x=6\) is valid.
questions.hint: After squaring, substitute each candidate back into the original equation; a nonnegative square root cannot equal a negative number.

questions.learningObjective: Solve a radical equation and use the domain to reject an extraneous candidate.
questions.question: Solve \(\sqrt{2x+7}=x+2\).
questions.explanation: Square both sides: \(2x+7=x^2+4x+4\). Then \(x^2+2x-3=0\), so \((x+3)(x-1)=0\). The candidates are \(x=-3\) and \(x=1\). Check \(x=-3\): \(\sqrt{1}=1\), but \(-3+2=-1\), so it is extraneous. Check \(x=1\): \(\sqrt{9}=3\), and \(1+2=3\). Thus only \(x=1\) is valid.
questions.hint: The right side \(x+2\) must be nonnegative because it equals a square root; check each candidate against the original equation.

questions.concept: Radical equations with two square roots
questions.learningObjective: Solve an equation containing two radicals by isolating one radical and squaring carefully.
questions.question: Solve \(\sqrt{x+6}-\sqrt{x-2}=2\).
questions.explanation:
Isolate one radical: \(\sqrt{x+6}=2+\sqrt{x-2}\). Square both sides:
\[
x+6=4+4\sqrt{x-2}+x-2
\]
Simplify: \(x+6=x+2+4\sqrt{x-2}\), so \(4=4\sqrt{x-2}\), giving \(\sqrt{x-2}=1\). Hence \(x-2=1\), so \(x=3\). Check: \(\sqrt{9}-\sqrt{1}=3-1=2\), so \(x=3\) is valid.
questions.hint: Isolate one radical first, then square both sides and simplify before squaring again if needed.

questions.concept: Solving radical equations with two radicals
questions.learningObjective: Solve an equation with two radical terms by isolating a radical and verifying the result.
questions.question: Solve \(\sqrt{x+5}+\sqrt{x-3}=4\).
questions.explanation:
Isolate one radical: \(\sqrt{x+5}=4-\sqrt{x-3}\). Square both sides:
\[
x+5=16-8\sqrt{x-3}+x-3
\]
Simplify: \(x+5=x+13-8\sqrt{x-3}\), so \(-8=-8\sqrt{x-3}\), giving \(\sqrt{x-3}=1\). Thus \(x-3=1\), so \(x=4\). Check: \(\sqrt{9}+\sqrt{1}=3+1=4\), so \(x=4\) is valid.
questions.hint: Move one radical to the right side, square, simplify, and then square again if necessary.

questions.concept: Radical equations with two valid solutions after verification
questions.learningObjective: Solve a radical equation with two radicals and verify that both solutions satisfy the original equation.
questions.question: Solve \(\sqrt{2x+3}-\sqrt{x+1}=1\).
questions.explanation:
Isolate one radical: \(\sqrt{2x+3}=1+\sqrt{x+1}\). Square both sides:
\[
2x+3=1+2\sqrt{x+1}+x+1
\]
Simplify: \(2x+3=x+2+2\sqrt{x+1}\), so \(x+1=2\sqrt{x+1}\). Let \(t=\sqrt{x+1}\), where \(t\ge0\). Then \(t^2=2t\), so \(t(t-2)=0\). Thus \(t=0\) or \(t=2\). Hence \(x+1=0\) or \(x+1=4\), giving \(x=-1\) or \(x=3\). Check \(x=-1\): \(\sqrt{1}-\sqrt{0}=1\). Check \(x=3\): \(\sqrt{9}-\sqrt{4}=3-2=1\). Both are valid.
questions.hint: Isolate one radical, square both sides, and then use substitution \(t=\sqrt{x+1}\) to solve the remaining equation.
